summary: Describes how to compress multiple IP headers, as well as TCP and UDP headers, hop by hop over point-to-point links. Shrinking the headers saves bandwidth, which matters most on slow links.

eli5.summary: Every internet message has a label on the front that repeats a lot of the same information. This document shows how to shorten the label so slow connections waste less time sending it.

questions: how to compress tcp and udp headers
how does tcp header compression recover from packet loss
what is a context identifier in header compression
how small can a compressed udp header get
subtitle: How to shrink IP, TCP and UDP headers to a few octets on slow or lossy point-to-point links, and keep working when packets are lost.

tldr.problem: On low and medium speed links, large IPv6 and IPv4 headers waste bandwidth and slow interactive traffic, yet the same header fields repeat almost unchanged from packet to packet.
tldr.mechanism: The sender (compressor) and receiver (decompressor) keep a shared context per packet stream, identified by a context identifier. A full header sets up the context, and later packets carry only the few fields that change.
tldr.outcome: Typical UDP or TCP headers shrink to 4-7 octets including the checksum. The design stays usable on lossy links by tagging non-TCP contexts with a generation, refreshing them periodically and repairing TCP contexts quickly.

today: RFC 2507 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The related documents it points to are RFC 2508 for compressing RTP headers and RFC 2509 for using it over PPP.

sections.title: Why Compress Headers
sections.content:
RFC 2507 describes how to compress multiple IP headers plus TCP and UDP headers, one hop at a time, over point-to-point links. It covers IPv6 base and extension headers, IPv4 headers, TCP and UDP headers, and encapsulated (tunneled) IPv6 and IPv4 headers.

The RFC gives several reasons to bother on low or medium speed links. It improves interactive response time, lets bulk data use small packets with good line efficiency, and helps delay-sensitive low-rate traffic such as voice. Its voice example: the smallest IPv6/UDP headers (48 octets) consume 19.2 kbit/s at 50 packets/s, and compression cuts that to about 1.7 kbit/s. It also lowers header overhead for IPv6/TCP from 19.5 per cent to less than 1 per cent, and because packets are smaller, fewer are lost for a given bit-error rate.

The idea rests on one observation: many header fields are constant or change in small, predictable steps between packets of the same stream. Constant fields need not be sent at all, predictable ones can be sent as a difference, and only fields that change randomly, such as checksums, travel in every header. The compression is explicitly designed to cope with links that lose packets, as several wireless and modem technologies do.
sections.eli5: Most of the label on each message is a copy of the one before. On a slow road, sending shorter labels means more room for the real stuff inside.

sections.title: Contexts, Identifiers and Packet Types
sections.content:
The scheme works by context: the state the compressor uses to compress and the decompressor uses to decompress, essentially the last header sent or received for a packet stream. A packet stream is a run of packets whose headers share things like source and destination addresses and port numbers. Each context is named by a context identifier (CID), a small number. CIDs can be 8 or 16 bits, and TCP and non-TCP contexts have separate CID spaces.

To start, the compressor sends a full header that carries a CID. Both ends store the fields as context. Later packets use compressed headers that give just the CID plus changes. If a field that is expected to stay constant changes, the compressor sends a full header again to update the context.

The method defines four packet types beyond ordinary IPv4 and IPv6 packets, and one extra type for feedback. Compression assumes the link does not reorder packets and that the link layer can report packet lengths with no padding added. If the link does reorder, the RFC provides separate mechanisms.

The RFC says IPv6 is not meant for links that deliver many damaged packets, and that compression SHOULD NOT be used for IPv4 without strong link-level checksums. The errors compression must handle are therefore packet loss, not bit corruption.
sections.eli5: The two ends of the line keep a shared notebook entry for each conversation. The first message fills in the entry, and after that they only say which entry and what changed.

sections.title: Staying in Sync When Packets Are Lost
sections.content:
Compression breaks if the two ends hold different contexts. TCP and non-TCP streams handle this differently.

For TCP, headers are compressed as a difference from the previous header, using the method of Van Jacobson in RFC 1144. A lost packet leaves the decompressor's context behind, so later headers decompress wrongly, but the TCP checksum catches the error and the receiver discards those segments. The compressor watches for TCP retransmissions and, when one occurs, sends a full header.

For UDP and other non-TCP streams there is no such safety net, so every version of the context carries a generation, a 6-bit number that increments whenever the context changes. Compressed headers carry the generation they were built with, and a decompressor discards (or briefly stores) any packet whose generation does not match. Because non-TCP compression does not use differences, losing a compressed header does not damage later ones. A compressor must not reuse a generation value in less than MIN_WRAP seconds, and MIN_WRAP is 3 seconds.

To recover from a lost full header without any handshake, the compressor uses compression slow-start and periodic refreshes. After a context change it sends a full header and sets F_PERIOD to one, then doubles F_PERIOD each time a full header is sent, up to F_MAX_PERIOD compressed headers between refreshes. A time limit, F_MAX_TIME, also forces a full header for slow streams. The RFC calls this a soft state scheme: it costs a bit more bandwidth than schemes that acknowledge every full header, but it needs no handshakes, so it works over simplex links such as direct-broadcast satellite.
sections.eli5: If a note in the shared notebook gets lost, the sender keeps re-copying the whole entry, first often, then less and less often. That way the other end catches up on its own without having to ask.

sections.title: Compressed Header Formats
sections.content:
A compressed non-TCP header starts with the CID, then a second octet holding a CID-size bit, a D bit and the 6-bit generation. If the CID is 16 bits long, its most and least significant octets sit on either side of that octet. If D is 1, one octet of data follows, and any RANDOM fields come after. With an 8-bit CID the minimum compressed non-TCP header is 2 octets.

A COMPRESSED_TCP header holds the CID, a flag octet with the bits R O I P S A W U, the TCP checksum, any RANDOM fields, and then optional fields for each flag that is set: an R-octet, urgent pointer value, window delta, acknowledgment number delta, sequence number delta, IPv4 identification delta and TCP options. The flags (apart from R and O) have the same meaning as in RFC 1144; the C bit is gone because the CID is always present.

A COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA header carries the CID, any RANDOM fields and the whole TCP header except the port numbers, with no differences used. Full headers avoid growing the packet by hiding the CID and generation in the length fields that already exist in the IP and UDP headers, since the link layer supplies the real packet length.
sections.eli5: A short label has a number saying which conversation, a few tick boxes for what changed, and then just the new values for the ticked boxes.

sections.title: How Each Header Field Is Treated
sections.content:
Section 7 walks through every field of every compressible subheader and classifies it. The four classes are NOCHANGE, DELTA, RANDOM and INFERRED. A compressed header never contains NOCHANGE or INFERRED fields. Any change in a NOCHANGE field means a full header MUST be sent.

For IPv6, the whole base header compresses away: version, flow label, next header, hop limit and the addresses are NOCHANGE and the payload length is INFERRED. Extension headers are mostly NOCHANGE too, so a Routing Header disappears completely, which matters because its maximum size is 392 octets. The Fragment Header compresses to 6 octets, and any subheaders after a Fragment Header MUST NOT be compressed. An Authentication Header's data is RANDOM, and after an ESP header everything is encrypted so nothing further can be compressed, except in tunnel mode where the inner packet may be compressed before it is encrypted.

A UDP header is typically compressed to just the 2-octet checksum, because ports are NOCHANGE and the length is INFERRED. A TCP header is either differentially encoded (sequence and acknowledgment numbers and window as DELTA, checksum RANDOM) or sent without differences as COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA. For IPv4, a plain header (no options, not a fragment) compresses well, while fragments or headers with options are sent with all fields as-is.

Grouping packets into streams is the compressor's job, and the RFC offers only optional guidelines, such as treating address, port and next-header fields as defining fields and never mixing fragments with unfragmented packets. Poor grouping gives bad compression but never incorrect decompression.
sections.eli5: Each part of the label is sorted: stays the same, changes by a little, changes wildly, or can be worked out from other things. Only the wild ones and tiny changes get sent.

sections.title: Fast Repair and Reordering
sections.content:
On a lossy link, one lost TCP segment can ruin a whole sending window of compressed headers. The RFC's example is a 2 Mbit/s wireless LAN with a 200 ms round trip, where a single loss can be multiplied by a factor of 100. It adds two repair mechanisms.

The twice algorithm lets the decompressor check the TCP checksum, and if it fails, add the current delta to the context again, on the assumption that the lost segment had the same delta. According to the RFC's traces this repairs between 83 and 99 per cent of single-segment losses in the data stream, and 53 to 99 per cent in the acknowledgment stream. When that fails, a decompressor on a two-way link MAY send a CONTEXT_STATE packet (type code 3) listing CIDs that are out of sync, and the compressor MUST then send a full header or a COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA header for them. Rate limiting these requests is a SHOULD.

Some links reorder packets. For non-TCP streams, a decompressor MAY keep both the old and new context for a while, and MUST discard the old one after MIN_WRAP seconds. For TCP, a compressor can send only NODELTA headers, but then compressed headers are typically 17 octets instead of 4-7. The better method adds a two-octet packet sequence number to each header, for a total of 6-9 octets. Sequence number zero MUST be skipped, and if a SYN segment carries the window scale option, the compressor MUST use packet sequence numbers for that stream.
sections.eli5: If a page of the shared notebook goes missing, the reader can guess the missing change and check it, or politely ask the sender to resend the whole page. If pages arrive out of order, numbering them puts them back in line.

sections.title: Link Layers and Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 2507 does not say how packets are labelled on a given link. Each link layer needs its own document, and one exists for PPP (RFC 2509). The RFC does suggest using bits of the IP Version field to mark full headers, whether the first subheader is IPv4 or IPv6, and whether the CID is for TCP. If a link cannot mark packet types, a leading octet can do it: 0 for COMPRESSED_TCP, 1 for COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA, 2 for COMPRESSED_NON_TCP and 3 for CONTEXT_STATE.

One parameter is fixed: MIN_WRAP is 3 seconds. The others are negotiated per link and have defaults, listed in the facts above. F_MAX_PERIOD defaults to 256, F_MAX_TIME to 5 seconds, MAX_HEADER to 168 octets, and both TCP_SPACE and NON_TCP_SPACE to 15 (16 CID values). MAX_HEADER caps how much of a header is stored as context, and an implementation MUST NOT partially compress a subheader.

A hook for further schemes lets the D bit and data octet carry a sequence number for compression layered on UDP, such as the compressed RTP of RFC 2508. Using such a scheme must be negotiated.
sections.eli5: Each kind of road has to write its own rules for how to spot a short label. The document gives sensible default settings, like how often to resend the full entry.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The compression runs on top of a link-layer protocol and introduces no new vulnerabilities beyond those of that link. The RFC does note that denial-of-service attacks are possible if an intruder can inject bogus full header packets, but says an intruder able to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer raises issues that dwarf those of header compression.

It also advises implementors against identifying packet streams using information that is encrypted, even when the compressor can see it, because doing so may expose traffic patterns.
sections.eli5: The shortcut does not open new doors for bad guys, but you should not peek at sealed envelopes to decide how to sort mail.

items.title: FULL_HEADER
items.text: An uncompressed header with a CID (and a generation for non-TCP). Sets up or refreshes the context.

items.title: COMPRESSED_NON_TCP
items.text: CID, generation and the randomly changing fields.

items.title: COMPRESSED_TCP
items.text: CID, a flag octet and changed fields as differences.

items.title: COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA
items.text: TCP fields sent as-is. Only sent in reply to a header request.

items.title: CONTEXT_STATE
items.text: Sent by the decompressor to list TCP CIDs that lost sync.

items.desc: Sent as-is in every compressed header.
